## (a) One-particle basis and spin-singlet states

Let r denote a site of the periodic cubic lattice, and let f ∈ {n,p} and s ∈ {↑,↓} denote nucleon flavor and spin. For dimensionless lattice momenta q = (2πm₁/L, 2πm₂/L, 2πm₃/L), define

a†_{q,f,s} = L^(-3/2) Σ_r exp(iq·r)c†_{r,f,s},   |q,f,s⟩ = a†_{q,f,s}|0⟩.

These states form a complete one-particle basis. A total-momentum-zero spin-singlet pair, for flavors f,g, can be written

|f g; q, S=0⟩ = (a†_{q,f,↑}a†_{−q,g,↓} − a†_{q,f,↓}a†_{−q,g,↑})|0⟩/√2.

In particular, the four flavor assignments are

|nn;q,0⟩ = (a†_{q,n↑}a†_{−q,n↓} − a†_{q,n↓}a†_{−q,n↑})|0⟩/√2,

|np;q,0⟩ = (a†_{q,n↑}a†_{−q,p↓} − a†_{q,n↓}a†_{−q,p↑})|0⟩/√2,

|pn;q,0⟩ = (a†_{q,p↑}a†_{−q,n↓} − a†_{q,p↓}a†_{−q,n↑})|0⟩/√2,

|pp;q,0⟩ = (a†_{q,p↑}a†_{−q,p↓} − a†_{q,p↓}a†_{−q,p↑})|0⟩/√2.

The creation operators enforce fermionic antisymmetry. The displayed normalization applies for generic q where the two terms are distinct orthogonal states. For identical flavors at q = −q modulo a reciprocal-lattice vector (in particular q=0), use the normalized state a†_{q,f,↑}a†_{q,f,↓}|0⟩ instead. Also avoid double-counting equivalent momentum/flavor assignments; for example, |np;q,0⟩ and |pn;−q,0⟩ describe the same state up to the fermionic operator ordering.

## (b) Matching the lattice kinetic energy

Fourier transforming the kinetic term gives the free-particle dispersion

ε(q) = 2t Σ_{i=1}^3 [1 − cos(q_i)].

The zero-momentum energy is zero, so it cannot fix t. The nontrivial matching is to the first nonzero mode, q=(2π/L,0,0), whose lattice energy is 2t[1−cos(2π/L)]. Its physical momentum is 2π/L_phy, with continuum nonrelativistic energy (2π/L_phy)²/(2M_phy). Therefore the exact finite-lattice matching is

t = (2π/L_phy)² / {4 M_phy [1 − cos(2π/L)]}.

Writing a=L_phy/L and expanding at small a (large L), 1−cos(2π/L) ≃ (2π/L)²/2, so

t → 1/(2M_phy a²).

This is the continuum-limit relation between the lattice hopping parameter and the physical mass.

## (c) Lowest nonzero single-particle energy

For L_phy=3.4 fm, M_phy=1634 MeV, and ℏc=197.32698 MeV·fm, the first nonzero physical momentum and its kinetic energy are

p_min = 2πℏc/L_phy ≃ 364.7 MeV,

E_min = p_min²/(2M_phy) ≃ (364.7 MeV)²/(3268 MeV) ≃ 40.7 MeV.

Thus the lowest nonzero single-particle energy is approximately 40.7 MeV. An exact finite-lattice energy would additionally require the number L of lattice sites; the value above is the physical continuum-box result.

## (d) Bound-state tuning and the first excitation

There is an important regulator issue. The onsite coupling C is a bare lattice coupling: its numerical value depends on the lattice spacing (equivalently, the ultraviolet cutoff). For example, at fixed lattice spacing and infinite volume, the total-momentum-zero bound-state equation for a two-neutron spin-singlet state with energy E=−B is

1 = −C ∫_{BZ} d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[B/t + 4Σ_i(1−cos q_i)],   B=17.8 MeV.

Here BZ is the dimensionless first Brillouin zone, and the equation follows from the rank-one onsite interaction Ct and the two-particle free energy 2ε(q)=4tΣ_i(1−cos q_i). Equivalently, for a specified lattice spacing,

C = −{∫_{BZ} d³q/(2π)³ · 1/[B/t + 4Σ_i(1−cos q_i)]}⁻¹.

Consequently a numerical bare C cannot be determined from B alone: the lattice spacing or cutoff must also be supplied. Taking the infinite-volume limit L→∞ at fixed spacing is not the same as taking the continuum limit a→0. In the continuum limit the bare coupling must be cutoff-dependently renormalized; there is no regulator-independent numerical bare C to report.

What the binding energy does fix in the zero-range continuum description is κ=√(MB) ≃ 170.5 MeV, since the relative kinetic energy of two equal-mass particles is k²/M. Under the zero-range assumption this corresponds to a positive scattering length 1/κ ≃ 1.16 fm.

The bound state is at −17.8 MeV. The two-body scattering spectrum begins at threshold E=0 and is continuous in infinite volume. Thus, if by the first excited energy one means the continuum threshold, it is 0 MeV, or 17.8 MeV above the bound-state energy. It is not a discrete first excited eigenstate in the thermodynamic limit.

## (e) Second excited state and degeneracy

There is no discrete second excited level in the stated infinite-volume limit: above the single bound state there is a continuum of scattering states with E≥0. Accordingly, no finite degeneracy can be assigned to a second excited level. A discrete second level and its degeneracy would require a specified finite box and a specified lattice spacing/interaction regulator; the resulting levels and shell degeneracies depend on those choices. This is why parts (d)–(e), if they require numerical C and discrete excited levels, are underdetermined as stated.
